title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Caching
summary: Defines HTTP caches and the header fields that control cache behavior or mark responses as cacheable. It was part of the revision of HTTP/1.1 that replaced RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9111.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7234 is the HTTP/1.1 specification for caching. It says which responses a cache is allowed to keep, how long a kept copy can be handed out without checking with the server, and how a cache checks with the server when the copy has gone out of date. It also defines the Cache-Control header, which both clients and servers use to state those rules.

questions: when can a response be cached
when is a cached response fresh
subtitle: How a copy of a web response is kept, when it may be reused, and how a server says when it must be checked again.

tldr.problem: The web repeats the same requests over and over, and fetching each one again from the origin server is slow and wasteful.
tldr.mechanism: A cache keeps a copy of a response and serves it again while it is fresh. When the copy has expired, the cache asks the origin server whether it is still valid, using a validator such as a Last-Modified date or an ETag, and refreshes its copy from the answer.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines when a response may be stored at all, how its age is calculated, and a set of Cache-Control directives for both ends to say what a cache may do. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9111.

today: RFC 7234 has been obsoleted by RFC 9111, so it is no longer a current standards document. It was published in June 2014 as part of the HTTP/1.1 revision that replaced RFC 2616, and it had itself obsoleted RFC 2616.

sections.title: What an HTTP Cache Is
sections.content:
HTTP is typically used for distributed information systems, where performance can be improved by the use of response caches. This document defines the parts of HTTP/1.1 that concern caching and reusing response messages.

An HTTP cache is a local store of response messages and the subsystem that controls storage, retrieval and deletion of messages in it. It stores cacheable responses in order to reduce the response time and network bandwidth consumption on future, equivalent requests. Any client or server may employ a cache, though a server that is acting as a tunnel cannot use one. A shared cache stores responses to be reused by more than one user and is usually deployed as part of an intermediary. A private cache is dedicated to a single user and is often deployed as part of a user agent.

The goal of caching in HTTP/1.1 is to improve performance significantly by reusing a prior response to satisfy a current request. A stored response is considered fresh if it can be reused without validation, which means checking with the origin server to see whether the cached response remains valid for this request. A fresh response reduces both latency and network overhead each time it is reused. A cached response that is not fresh might still be reusable, either because it can be freshened by validation or because the origin is unavailable.

Proper cache operation preserves the semantics of HTTP transfers while eliminating the transfer of information the cache already holds. Caching is an entirely optional feature, but reusing a cached response is desirable and is the default when nothing prevents it, so the requirements are aimed at preventing a cache from storing a response that cannot be reused or from reusing a stored one inappropriately. Each cache entry consists of a cache key and one or more responses for prior requests that used the same key. The most common form is a 200 response to a GET request, but permanent redirects, negative results such as 404, incomplete results such as 206, and responses to other methods may also be cached. The primary cache key is the request method and the target URI, though many caches only cache GET responses and use just the URI. When a request target is subject to content negotiation, its cache entry may hold several stored responses, each distinguished by a secondary key holding the values of the original request's selecting header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache is a box of saved answers. When the same question is asked again, the answer comes out of the box instead of from the far end of the network. The rules exist so that a cache never hands back something that has gone out of date without first finding out whether it still applies.

sections.title: When a Response May Be Stored
sections.content:
A cache must not store a response unless several conditions hold. The request method must be one the cache understands and that is defined as cacheable, and the response status code must be one the cache understands. The no-store directive must not appear in the request or the response. The private response directive must not appear in the response if the cache is shared. The Authorization header field must not appear in the request if the cache is shared, unless the response explicitly allows such responses to be stored. And the response must either carry an Expires header field, carry a max-age directive, carry an s-maxage directive when the cache is shared, carry a cache control extension that allows it to be cached, have a status code that is cacheable by default, or carry a public directive.

Any of those requirements can be overridden by a cache-control extension. In normal operation some caches will not store a response that has neither a cache validator nor an explicit expiration time, since such responses are not usually useful to store, but the specification does not forbid it.

An incomplete response is one where the connection closed before all the octets the framing indicated were received. If the method is GET, the status is 200 and the whole header section has arrived, a cache may store the incomplete body provided the entry is recorded as incomplete; a 206 response may be stored the same way. A cache must not store incomplete or partial-content responses if it does not support the Range and Content-Range header fields or does not understand the range units used in them. A cache must not use an incomplete response to answer a request unless it has been completed or the request asks for a range wholly inside it, and it must not send a partial response to a client without marking it with the 206 status code.

Authenticated requests get extra protection. A shared cache must not use a cached response to a request carrying an Authorization header field to satisfy any later request, unless a directive in the response allows it. The directives that have that effect are must-revalidate, public and s-maxage. Responses carrying must-revalidate or s-maxage also cannot be served stale by shared caches, so a response with either max-age=0, must-revalidate or s-maxage=0 cannot satisfy a later request without being revalidated at the origin.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a list of reasons a cache must refuse to keep an answer: the server asked it not to, the answer is personal, the request was authenticated, or there is no way to tell when the answer goes out of date. A half-received answer may be kept, but only if the cache knows how to finish it.

sections.title: Serving and Validating a Stored Response
sections.content:
A cache must not reuse a stored response unless the presented effective request URI matches the stored one, the stored response's request method allows it to be used for the presented request, the selecting header fields the stored response nominates match, the presented request contains neither the no-cache pragma nor the no-cache directive unless the stored response is successfully validated, the stored response does not itself carry the no-cache directive unless it is validated, and the stored response is fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated.

When a stored response is used without validation, the cache must generate an Age header field, replacing any present, holding the stored response's current age. A cache must write through requests with unsafe methods, which means it may not generate a reply before it has forwarded the request and received the matching response; such requests might also invalidate responses the cache already holds. When more than one suitable response is stored, the cache must use the most recent one, as determined by the Date header field, and it can forward the request with max-age=0 or no-cache to disambiguate. A cache with no working clock must not use stored responses without revalidating them on every use.

The selecting header fields, and so the secondary key, come from the Vary header field. When a stored response has a Vary, the cache must not use it unless all the fields Vary nominates match in both the original request and the presented one. Two requests' selecting fields match only if the first can be transformed into the second by adding or removing whitespace where the syntax allows it, by combining multiple header fields with the same name, or by normalizing both values in a way known to have identical semantics, such as reordering where order does not matter or case-normalizing where values are case-insensitive. A field absent from a request after normalization can only match another request where it is also absent. A Vary value of * always fails to match. If several responses are selected, a known mechanism such as qvalues on Accept may pick a preferred one, and of the remainder the most recent is used. If no response is selected, the request goes to the origin server.

When a cache holds responses for a requested URI but cannot serve any of them, because they are stale or because none can be selected, it can use the conditional request mechanism in the forwarded request. That gives the next inbound server the chance to confirm that a stored response is still equivalent to the current representation, updating the stored metadata in the process, or to replace it with a new response. The validators used are the timestamp in a Last-Modified header field, which can go in If-Modified-Since for validation or in If-Unmodified-Since or If-Range for selecting a representation, and the entity-tag in an ETag header field, which can go in If-None-Match for validation or in If-Match or If-Range for selecting a representation.

A cache that receives a conditional request must evaluate the applicable preconditions against the validators in the response it has selected, but must not evaluate preconditions that only apply to an origin server, that belong to a request whose semantics cannot be met from a cache, or that apply to a resource the cache holds nothing for; those are probably meant for another server. The If-Match and If-Unmodified-Since fields are not applicable to a cache at all. When the answer comes back, a 304 means the stored response can be updated and reused, a full response means none of the nominated stored responses was suitable, so the cache must use the full response and may replace what it had, and a 5xx leaves the cache free either to forward the error or to treat it as a failure to respond, in which case it may send a stored response instead.
sections.plainLanguage: When the stored copy has gone stale, the cache sends the request on with a note asking whether the page it already has is still the current one. The server answers with a short not modified message, and the cache refreshes its copy from the metadata that came back, or with the whole new answer if the page really did change.

sections.title: Freshness, Age and Stale Responses
sections.content:
A response is fresh when its age has not yet passed its freshness lifetime, and stale when it has. The freshness lifetime is the length of time between the response being generated by the origin server and its expiration time. An explicit expiration time is the moment the origin server intends the response to stop being usable without further validation; a heuristic expiration time is one a cache assigns when the server gave no explicit time. The age of a response is the time since it was generated by, or successfully validated with, the origin server.

The main way freshness is set is for the origin server to give an explicit expiration time in the future, with either the Expires header field or the max-age directive. A server that wants every request validated can set the expiration time in the past, and a compliant cache will then validate a stale response before reusing it. The test is simply whether the freshness lifetime is greater than the current age. Clients can send the max-age or min-fresh directives to constrain or relax the calculation.

The freshness lifetime is calculated by taking the first of these that applies: the s-maxage value, if the cache is shared and s-maxage is present; the max-age value, if max-age is present; the Expires value minus the Date value, if Expires is present; and otherwise nothing explicit, in which case a heuristic may apply. Because all the information comes from the origin server, this calculation is not vulnerable to clock skew. If more than one value is present for a directive, the directive's value is considered invalid, and caches are encouraged to treat a response with invalid freshness information as stale.

A cache may assign a heuristic expiration time when the server gave none, using other header values such as the Last-Modified time to estimate a plausible one. The specification gives no algorithm but imposes worst-case limits: heuristics must not be used when an explicit expiration time is present, and when the response has a Last-Modified field, the heuristic value should be no more than some fraction of the interval since that time, a typical setting being 10 per cent. A cache that uses a heuristic should add a Warning header field with the 113 warn-code when the response is more than 24 hours old.

The Age header field carries the sender's estimate of the time since the response was generated or validated at the origin server. In essence the value is the sum of the time the response has spent in each cache along the path plus the time in transit. It is computed from the Age field already present, the Date field, the time the request was made and the time the response arrived: the apparent age is the response time minus the date value, floored at zero; the response delay is the response time minus the request time; the corrected age value is the incoming Age value plus that delay; and the corrected initial age is the larger of the apparent age and the corrected age value, unless the cache trusts the Age field, in which case it may use the corrected age value alone. The current age adds the time the response has been resident in the cache since it arrived.

A cache must not generate a stale response if an explicit directive forbids it, such as no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, or an applicable s-maxage or proxy-revalidate. It must not send stale responses at all unless it is disconnected from the origin or the request explicitly allows it, for example with the max-stale directive. A cache should add the 110 warn-code to stale responses, and the 112 warn-code when it is disconnected.
sections.plainLanguage: Freshness is a simple comparison: how old is this copy, against how long is it good for. The server normally says how long, the cache works out how old, and if the numbers say the copy is too old the cache has to check with the server before handing it out.

sections.title: The Directives That Control Caching
sections.content:
The Cache-Control header field carries directives for caches along the request and response chain. Such directives are unidirectional: a directive in a request does not imply the same directive in the response. A proxy, whether or not it implements a cache, must pass cache directives through in forwarded messages, and it is not possible to target a directive at a particular cache.

The request-side directives are max-age, which says the client will not accept a response older than the given number of seconds, and, unless max-stale is also present, will not accept a stale response at all; max-stale, which says the client will accept a response that has exceeded its freshness lifetime, by no more than the given number of seconds if a value is given or of any age if not; min-fresh, which says the client wants a response that will still be fresh for at least the given number of seconds; no-cache, which says the cache must not use a stored response without validating it at the origin; no-store, which says the cache must not store any part of the request or of the response, and which is explicitly not a reliable privacy mechanism; no-transform, which says an intermediary must not transform the payload; and only-if-cached, which says the client wants only a stored response, so the cache should answer from its store if it can and otherwise return a 504 Gateway Timeout.

The response-side directives are must-revalidate, which says a stale response cannot be reused without successful validation, and which a cache must obey in all circumstances, generating a 504 if it cannot reach the origin server at all; no-cache, which says the response cannot be used to satisfy a later request without validation, and which, when it lists field names, means those header fields must not be sent again without revalidation while the rest of the response may be; no-store; no-transform; public, which lets any cache store the response even where it would normally not be allowed to; private, which says the response is for a single user and must not be stored by a shared cache, or, when it lists field names, protects only those fields; proxy-revalidate, which means the same as must-revalidate but does not apply to private caches; max-age, which says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds; and s-maxage, which in shared caches overrides both max-age and Expires and implies proxy-revalidate.

The Expires header field gives the date and time after which the response is considered stale. Its presence says nothing about whether the resource will change or stop existing. A cache recipient must read an invalid date, including the value 0, as a time in the past. If a response carries max-age, the Expires field must be ignored, and if it carries s-maxage, a shared cache must ignore it as well. The Pragma header field exists for backwards compatibility with HTTP/1.0 caches: when Cache-Control is present and understood, Pragma is ignored, and when it is absent, a no-cache pragma has the same effect as a no-cache directive. A cache may add extension directives, and must ignore any it does not recognise.

The Warning header field carries extra information about the status or transformation of a message that the status code does not reflect, typically to warn about possible incorrectness introduced by caching. Using a warning rather than an error code distinguishes these responses from true failures. Warn codes have three digits, and the first digit says whether the warning must be deleted from a stored response after validation: 1xx codes describe freshness or validation status and must be deleted, and can only be generated by a cache while validating; 2xx codes describe an aspect of the representation that validation does not fix and must not be deleted unless a full response is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends can state rules with Cache-Control. The client can say how old an answer it will accept; the server can say how long the answer may be kept, whether it may be kept by a shared cache, and whether it must be checked even when it looks usable. The older Pragma and Expires headers exist for the same job and for compatibility with HTTP/1.0.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Caches expose additional potential vulnerabilities, because their contents are an attractive target and they persist after an HTTP request is complete. An attack on a cache can reveal information long after a user believes the information has left the network, so cache contents need to be protected as sensitive information.

Attacks may be amplified by being stored in a shared cache. Cache poisoning attacks use the cache to distribute a malicious payload to many clients, and are especially effective when an attacker can use implementation flaws, elevated privileges or other techniques to insert such a response into a cache. One common vector is to exploit differences in message parsing between proxies and user agents. Implementation flaws, or a misunderstanding of how caches operate, may also lead to sensitive information such as authentication credentials being cached although it was thought to be private.

The use of a cache brings privacy concerns of its own. If two users share a cache and the first browses to a site, the second may be able to detect that the first has been there, because the resources from it load more quickly. The Set-Cookie response header field does not inhibit caching: a cacheable response that carries a Set-Cookie field can be, and often is, used to satisfy later requests, so servers that want to control this are encouraged to send appropriate Cache-Control response header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared cache is a place where answers from one user can be handed to another, so it needs care. It also makes a good target: one poisoned answer can reach many people at once, and it keeps a copy of things long after the user thinks they have gone.

viz.caption: A CACHE VALIDATING A STORED RESPONSE

messages.label: GET /resource
messages.note: The client asks for the resource.

messages.label: GET /resource, conditional
messages.note: The stored copy is stale, so the cache forwards the request with a validator such as If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since.

messages.label: 304 Not Modified
messages.note: The origin says the copy the cache holds is still current.

messages.label: 200 OK with Age
messages.note: The cache serves the stored copy and adds an Age header saying how old it is.

items.title: no-store
items.text: The cache must not store any part of the request or the response. It is not a reliable privacy mechanism.

items.title: private
items.text: The response is for a single user and must not be stored by a shared cache. With field names, only those fields are protected.

items.title: public
items.text: Any cache may store the response, even one that would normally not be allowed to.

items.title: must-revalidate
items.text: Once stale, the response cannot be reused without checking with the origin server. A cache that cannot reach the origin must answer 504.

items.title: max-age
items.text: The response is stale once its age is greater than this many seconds.

items.title: s-maxage
items.text: In shared caches this overrides max-age and Expires, and it implies proxy-revalidate.

viz.caption: THE WARNING CODES DEFINED BY THE RFC

items.label: Response is Stale
items.desc: A cache should generate this whenever the response it sends is stale.

items.label: Revalidation Failed
items.desc: A cache should generate this when sending a stale response because it could not reach the server to validate it.

items.label: Disconnected Operation
items.desc: A cache should generate this if it is intentionally disconnected from the rest of the network.

items.label: Heuristic Expiration
items.desc: A cache should generate this if it guessed a freshness lifetime over 24 hours and the response is older than that.

items.label: Transformation Applied
items.desc: A proxy must add this if it transforms the representation.

items.label: Miscellaneous Persistent Warning
items.desc: Arbitrary information for a person or a log. A receiving system must take no automated action.
